absent: No participatory action research literature, no critical or feminist political ecology, and nothing on caste or gender in water access, though the framework assigns duties to users.
forYou: A worked example of building a framework from a non-Western philosophical source while keeping analytic discipline — useful as a model, and as a target, for your pluriversal work.
method: References read from the article text; strands and narrative by Claude, grounded only in those citations.
narrative: The root is Ostrom (1990, 2005) and the commons tradition: communities can govern shared resources without state or market, under structural conditions.

The paper's move is to say that this tradition, along with adaptive governance (Pahl-Wostl 2007) and the OECD principles (2015), treats moral orientation as something institutions draw on rather than form. Motivation-crowding work (Frey & Jegen 2001; Bowles 2008) supplies the mechanism for why that matters.

Its distinctive resource is the Bhagavad Gita in Sargeant's translation, read alongside Indian management scholarship (Chakraborty 1995; Bhawuk 2011) and balanced by Leopold (1949) and Groenfeldt (2013) so the argument is not framed as East versus West. The hydrology (Jasechko et al. 2024; Grafton et al. 2018; Shah 2009) carries the problem statement.
